extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (curves)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and classification criteria for algebraic curves by genus (0–5 and general statements), hyperelliptic property, canonical embeddings, and related constructions and moduli heuristics. Contains definitions, theorems, propositions, and exercises that give concrete criteria for recognizing and constructing curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 0 curves as conics in P2_k (Claim 19.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: All genus 0 curves can be described as conics in P2_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any genus 0 curve has a degree −2 line bundle — the dualizing sheaf ω_C. Thus any genus 0 curve has a degree 2 line bundle L = ω_C^∨. By Remark 19.2.11 (deg L = 2) this line bundle gives a closed embedding into P2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a low-degree point on genus 0 curve (Exercise 19.3.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose C is a genus 0 curve (projective, geometrically integral and regular). Show that C has a point of degree at most 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of a point defined earlier (5.3.8). This is an arithmetic consequence of genus 0 geometry: genus 0 curves have low-degree closed points (≤2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: h0(L) < 2 for degree 1 line bundle on non-P1 curve (Proposition 19.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a projective, geometrically regular, geometrically integral curve over k not isomorphic to P1_k, and L is an invertible sheaf of degree 1, then h0(C, L) < 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: two independent sections would vanish at single points p1 and p2; if p1 != p2, the sections give a base-point-free linear series giving a finite degree-1 morphism C → P1, hence an isomorphism — contradiction. Thus a degree-1 line bundle has at most one (up to scalar) section on such C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of degree-1 line bundles from points (Corollary 19.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a projective, geometrically regular, geometrically integral curve over k not isomorphic to P1_k and p and q are degree 1 points, then O_C(p) ≅ O_C(q) if and only if p = q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from Proposition 19.4.1: degree 1 line bundles have exactly one section and distinct points give distinct line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bezout/Cayley-Bacharach-type uniqueness for plane curves meeting C (Exercise 19.4.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose C is a regular plane curve of degree e > 2, and D1 and D2 are two plane curves of the same degree d not containing C. By Bézout's Theorem, Di meets C at de points. Suppose D1 and D2 meet C at de − 1 of the 'same points', plus one more; show the remaining points are the same as well (more precisely: if there is a divisor E on C of degree de − 1 and degree 1 k-valued points p1 and p2 with C = E + p_i as divisors, show p1 = p2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an elementary form of Cayley–Bacharach/Chasles: enough common intersection points force equality of the remaining point; the exercise points toward classical intersection-theoretic uniqueness statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus's Theorem (19.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two distinct lines ℓ and m and distinct points α, β, γ on ℓ and α', β', γ' on m (all six points distinct from ℓ ∩ m), define x = αβ' ∩ αγ', y = α'β ∩ α'γ, z = βγ' ∩ β'γ. Then x, y, z are collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented here as a classical geometry consequence derived from algebraic-geometry methods; proof relates to degeneration of Pascal's Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's 'Mystical Hexagon' Theorem (19.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hexagon αγ'βα'γβ' is inscribed in a smooth conic K, and opposite pairs of sides are extended until they meet, then the three intersection points x = αβ' ∩ αγ', y = α'β ∩ α'γ, and z = βγ' ∩ β'γ are collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses algebraic-geometry methods: consider unions of lines and conics, apply earlier propositions/corollaries (e.g., Prop. 19.4.1 and Cor. 19.4.2) possibly extending to singular curves via normalization and scheme-theoretic arguments (nilpotents). Pappus is a degeneration of Pascal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: hyperelliptic curve (section 19.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective regular integral genus g curve C is hyperelliptic if it admits a double cover (degree 2 finite morphism) π : C → P1_k. When g ≥ 2, such a double cover (if it exists) is at most unique (Proposition 19.5.7). The map π is called the hyperelliptic map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (Exercise 19.5.B), for g ≥ 1, C is hyperelliptic iff it admits a degree 2 invertible sheaf L with h0(C, L) = 2; such an L is base-point-free and gives the hyperelliptic map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperelliptic Riemann–Hurwitz formula (Theorem 19.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume k is algebraically closed of characteristic not 2. If π : C → P1_k is a double cover by a projective regular irreducible genus g curve, then π has 2g + 2 branch points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Riemann–Hurwitz formula specialized to degree-2 covers; a concrete proof is given by explicit models y^2 = f(x) and genus computation via Čech cohomology (see 19.5.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of double covers of P1 by branch points and explicit model (Proposition 19.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume char k ≠ 2 and k algebraically closed. Given r distinct points p1,...,pr ∈ P1 (or A1) there is precisely one double cover branched at precisely these points if r is even; the cover is given (over an affine patch A1 = Spec k[x]) by y^2 = f(x) where f(x) = (x − p1)···(x − pr) is monic with no repeated roots, and appropriate gluing gives the global curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction proceeds by taking quadratic field extension K/k(x) generated by y with σ(y) = −y, arranging y^2 ∈ k[x] monic without repeated factors, showing normalization of A1 in that extension gives the curve, and analyzing behavior on the other affine patch u = 1/x. If r is even there is a unique gluing; if r odd, one must consider extra phenomena (Exercise 19.5.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twists/classification over non-algebraically-closed fields (19.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is not algebraically closed (char ≠ 2), a double cover over A1 is of the form y^2 = a f(x) for a ∈ k×, and two such covers y^2 = a f(x) and y^2 = a' f(x) are isomorphic over k if and only if a and a' differ by an element of (k×)^2; failure of determination by branch points is measured by k×/(k×)^2 (twists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the arithmetic subtleties: branch points determine the cover over algebraic closure, but over k there are distinct isomorphism classes (twists) parametrized by quadratic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus formula for double cover via Čech computation (19.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a double cover of P1 given by y^2 = f(x) where deg f = r, the genus g of the normalization C is g = r/2 − 1 (computed by analyzing the Čech complex for O_C and counting monomials x^n y^ε that survive in the cokernel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit algebraic computation completes the proof of the hyperelliptic Riemann–Hurwitz formula in this setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of hyperelliptic cover for g ≥ 2 (Proposition 19.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any curve C of genus at least 2 admits at most one double cover of P1. More precisely, if L and M are two degree-two line bundles yielding maps C → P1, then L ≅ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof recovers the hyperelliptic map from the canonical linear series ω_C: composition with the (g−1)th Veronese yields the rational normal curve and recovers the double cover uniquely; apply Theorem 16.4.1 to relate maps to line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli/count of hyperelliptic curves (19.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperelliptic curves of genus g ≥ 2 correspond to precisely 2g + 2 distinct points on P1 modulo S_{2g+2} and modulo automorphisms of P1; heuristically the 'space of hyperelliptic curves' has dimension 2g − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a plausibility/moduli count: number of branch points minus automorphism parameters. The statement is heuristic pending a rigorous moduli-space construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 2 curves are hyperelliptic and classification (19.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve C of genus 2, ω_C has degree 2 and has 2 sections, hence is base-point-free and induces a double cover C → P1; conversely any degree-2 invertible sheaf with at least 2 sections is the dualizing sheaf. Thus genus 2 curves biject with genus-2 double covers of P1 (up to automorphisms of P1); in char ≠ 2 these are branched over 6 points (so a three-dimensional family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 19.2.A and Exercise 19.5.B for the equivalence between degree-2 line bundles with h0=2 and hyperelliptic maps. Provides dimension/count heuristic and consequences (finite automorphism group Exercise 19.6.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical linear series for genus 3: base-point-free and embedding criterion (19.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a genus 3 curve C, ω_C has degree 4 and h0(ω_C) = 3. The invertible sheaf ω_C is base-point-free and hence gives a map to P2. This map is a closed embedding iff C is not hyperelliptic; if not hyperelliptic then C is a degree-4 plane curve (quartic) canonically embedded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check base-point-freeness via Riemann–Roch and Prop. 19.4.1. If ω_C fails to be an embedding one finds a degree-2 divisor with two sections implying hyperellipticity. Conversely, any quartic plane curve has genus 3 and is mapped by the unique degree-4 line bundle with three sections, hence is canonical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection: nonhyperelliptic genus 3 curves ↔ plane quartics (19.7.1 conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each nonhyperelliptic genus 3 curve can be described as a plane quartic in only one way (up to automorphisms of P2), and conversely regular plane quartics give nonhyperelliptic genus 3 curves. Thus there is a bijection between nonhyperelliptic genus 3 curves and plane quartic curves up to projective linear transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies geometric models for genus 3 curves and explains counts/dimension heuristics (family dimension 6 up to PGL(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical description of nonhyperelliptic genus 4 curves as complete intersections (19.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonhyperelliptic genus 4 curve C has deg ω_C = 6 and h0(ω_C) = 4, so the canonical map embeds C as a degree-6 curve in P3. There exists at least one quadric surface Q in P3 containing C; moreover C is the complete intersection of such a quadric Q and a cubic surface K (i.e., C = Q ∩ K) and conversely any regular complete intersection of a quadric and cubic in P3 is a canonically embedded genus 4 curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension counts (h0), Bézout's theorem, and Hilbert polynomial/genus considerations are used to find Q and K and show equality of Hilbert polynomials; Exercise 19.8.C checks that O_C(1) has ≥4 sections and hence equals ω_C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical genus 5 curves and quadrics (19.8.E–F)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonhyperelliptic genus 5 canonical curve is degree 8 in P4 and lies on a three-dimensional vector space of quadrics (i.e., on 3 linearly independent quadrics). A regular complete intersection of three quadrics in P4 is a canonically embedded genus 5 curve. Most canonical genus 5 curves are such complete intersections; exceptions are precisely the trigonal curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigonality (degree-3 map to P1) gives the exceptional locus: three points mapping to same point in P1 lie on a line in the canonical embedding forcing quadrics vanishing on these points to vanish on that line. Heuristic family dimension count gives dim ≈ 12 for genus 5 curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-complete-intersection canonical curves for g ≥ 6 (19.8.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C ⊂ P^{g−1} is a canonical curve of genus g ≥ 6 then C is not necessarily a complete intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simple complete-intersection descriptions valid in low genus break down for higher genus; Exercise hint suggests using Bézout-type arguments to show canonical curves fail to be complete intersections in general for g ≥ 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli dimension heuristic: dim M_g = 3g − 3 for g > 1 (19.8.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic/known fact: for g > 1 the (ill-defined here) moduli space M_g of genus g curves has dimension 3g − 3. Exceptions in low genus explained by larger automorphism groups: genus 0 curve has 3-dimensional automorphism group, genus 1 curves have 1-dimensional automorphism groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heuristic arises by counting parameters for canonical embeddings, subtracting automorphism dimensions; in stack language dim M0 = −3, dim M1 = 0, etc. The text sketches the reasoning without full moduli-space machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line bundles on genus 1 curves: ω_C and degree formulas (19.9.1–2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a genus 1 curve C, deg ω_C = 0 and h0(ω_C) = 1; ω_C ≅ O_C (the structure sheaf). For any line bundle L with deg L > 0, Riemann-Roch and Serre duality give h0(C, L) = deg L. Degree-1 line bundles correspond bijectively to degree-1 points: every degree-1 line bundle L is O(q) for its unique zero divisor q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts lead into the definition of elliptic curves: an elliptic curve is a genus 1 curve with a choice of k-valued point p (the basepoint is part of the data). Twisting degree-1 bundles by O(−p) gives a bijection between degree-0 invertible sheaves and degree-1 points; the degree-0 line bundles form a group under tensor product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: degree-2 line bundle with two sections ↔ hyperelliptic (Exercise 19.5.B/19.5.B commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose C is a curve of genus at least 1. Then C admits a degree-2 cover of P1 if and only if it admits a degree-2 invertible sheaf L with h0(C, L) = 2. Moreover, such an L (with exactly two independent sections) is base-point-free and gives the hyperelliptic map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a sheaf-theoretic criterion to detect hyperellipticity, useful in proofs of uniqueness (19.5.7) and in explicit constructions.
